"Supposed" is an adjective that signals doubt about a label or claim. When you describe something as "supposed," you're saying: "This is what people believe or claim it to be — but it may not actually be true."

Think of it as placing invisible quotation marks around a description. You're not saying something is definitely wrong. You're simply distancing yourself from the claim, or flagging that the claim is unproven.

This is the purest adjective use of the word. "Supposed" comes directly before a noun to cast doubt on the description given to that person or thing.

Examples:

  • "The police arrested the supposed leader of the gang."

The police believe he is the leader — but it hasn't been proven in court. The word "supposed" keeps the claim cautious and fair.

  • "She spent her savings on a supposed miracle cure."

The product was marketed as a miracle cure. The speaker doubts it truly is one.

  • "My supposed best friend never showed up when I needed help."

He called himself a best friend. His actions suggest otherwise. Here, "supposed" carries a tone of disappointment and irony.

The feeling this creates: A quiet skepticism. You're not loudly calling something fake — you're simply raising an eyebrow at the label it has been given.

Important: In this sense, "supposed" almost always comes before the noun, not after it. You say "a supposed expert," not "the expert is supposed" (that would mean something different, as you'll see below).
Sense 2: "Be Supposed To" — The Phrasal Form

"Supposed" is also used constantly in the phrase "be supposed to." This is a different but equally important use, and it has three distinct meanings. You must know all three to truly understand this word.

2a. Expected or Required to Do Something

This is probably the most common use in everyday English. It means someone is expected, required, or obligated to do something — based on a rule, an agreement, someone's instructions, or a plan.

  • "You are supposed to wear a seatbelt while driving." (The law requires it.)
  • "He was supposed to call me at 8, but he never did." (I expected him to — he didn't.)
  • "I'm supposed to submit this report by Friday." (That's the deadline set for me.)

Notice the feeling here: there is often a gap between what someone is supposed to do and what they actually do. The word highlights that gap, or sets the expectation clearly.

2b. Generally Believed or Said to Be True

Here, "supposed to" means: "People say this, or it has this reputation — though I haven't confirmed it myself."

  • "This restaurant is supposed to be excellent." (I haven't been there, but that's what people say.)
  • "The book is supposed to be very difficult." (That's its reputation.)
  • "He is supposed to be one of the wealthiest people in the city." (That's what people believe.)

This meaning is closely related to Sense 1. The difference is small: in Sense 1 ("a supposed expert"), doubt is in the speaker's mind. In this sense ("he is supposed to be an expert"), the belief is attributed to people in general — the speaker is reporting what others think, while staying somewhat neutral.

2c. Allowed or Permitted (Usually in Negative Sentences)

In negative sentences, "supposed to" takes on a meaning of permission — specifically, something that is not allowed.

  • "You are not supposed to smoke in this building." (It is not permitted here.)
  • "We weren't supposed to know about the surprise party." (We weren't meant to find out.)
  • "She is not supposed to leave the hospital yet." (The doctor has not cleared her to do so.)

Here, "not supposed to" is a gentle but clear way of saying something is against the rules, against someone's wishes, or simply not intended.

Supposed vs. Actual/Real:
These are near-opposites. "Actual" means genuinely what it is called. "Supposed" means only claimed or believed to be what it is called — with doubt hanging over it.

  • "The supposed advantages of the plan were never proven." (Claimed, but not real.)
  • "The actual advantages became clear over time." (Genuinely real.)

Supposed vs. So-called:
Both carry skepticism, but they differ in sharpness. "Supposed" is relatively measured — you're expressing doubt. "So-called" is more dismissive or even sarcastic — you're strongly implying the label is wrong or ridiculous.

  • "a supposed expert" → Maybe he is, maybe he isn't. I'm not sure.
  • "a so-called expert" → He calls himself an expert, but I very much doubt it.
A Very Common Spelling Mistake to Avoid

Many people write "suppose to" instead of "supposed to." This is an error. The correct form always has the -d at the end: supposed to. Even though the d is barely heard in spoken English (since it blurs into the t of "to"), it must always be written.

✗ "You are suppose to be here by now."
✓ "You are supposed to be here by now."

"Supposed" is a word of caution and precision. It lets you describe something without fully committing to the claim. This is why journalists use it ("the supposed attacker"), lawyers use it ("the supposed contract"), and careful speakers use it every day. In ordinary conversation, it lets you express doubt or disappointment — subtly and elegantly — without making a harsh accusation.

When someone says "my supposed friend", you immediately understand there is hurt or sarcasm behind it. When a headline says "the supposed cure," you know to be skeptical. That is the quiet but powerful work this word does.
